findings.issue_text: [BUG] `validates :email, email: true` raises 'Unknown validator: EmailValidator' at class load / first validation because the validator lives at lib/validators/email_validator.rb, which resolves to the constant `Validators::EmailValidator`, not `EmailValidator`, and `lib/validators` is not an autoload path suffix where `EmailValidator` can be found. Instantiating or validating any User (every signup, every save that changes email) raises NameError/ArgumentError from the unknown validator, so account creation is completely broken in this diff as written; the validator must be moved to a path whose constant name matches (e.g. app/validators or lib/email_validator.rb) or required/aliased explicitly.

[ADVISORY] `BlockedEmail.should_block?` executes `record.save` (a DB write) inside model validation of an unrelated User record, so signup attempts write statistics on every validation pass. Operators see match_count and last_match_at inflated by multiple validation passes per signup attempt (and by re-submissions that fail other validations), corrupting the blocking statistics the table exists to collect; it also makes User validation non-idempotent and couples it to a second table's write path.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin controller, UI, rake task, or seed populates it, only spec fabricators. After deploying this diff, the feature is inert: admins have no way to add a blocked email, so every user signs up normally and the new validation, migration, and client-side rejectedEmails plumbing are dead code until a follow-up ships an interface.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email check is gated on `if: :email_changed?`, so an existing User whose email is unchanged never runs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` — but since email only changes via assignment this gate also skips the check on every subsequent save of a user whose email was set in the same save cycle before validation, depending on when `email_changed?` is evaluated relative to attribute assignment in each caller. Admins who block an address after a user registered with it see no enforcement on that user's later profile saves, and developers reading the diff assume the whitelist/blacklist semantics carried over exactly, when the previous `email_validator` was likewise conditional — mostly a comprehension/hidden-coupling smell in the conditional placement rather than a new behavior break, but the next change to email update flows has to reason about validation ordering twice.

[BUG] Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive, so a blocked address is bypassed by any case variant of the local part or domain. A user (or spammer) entering Bad@Spamclub.com when the blocked_emails row stores bad@spamclub.com passes validation and registers; nothing in this diff downcases the value before the BlockedEmail lookup (email_in_restriction_setting? only escapes dots), and no test covers mixed case.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (record.save for match_count/last_match_at) inside model validation, so the statistics update is rolled back whenever the surrounding user save fails. The user create always fails when the email is blocked (that is the point of the block), so the whole transaction — including the should_block? save — rolls back and match_count/last_match_at never persist on the blocked-registration path the feature exists to track; the spec's 'updates statistics' example only passes because it calls should_block? directly outside a transaction.

[ADVISORY] The client discards the server's specific error message for blocked emails and shows the generic 'user.email.invalid' string. The server adds a distinct 'user.email.blocked' locale ('is not allowed.') and returns errors.email in the JSON, but the rejected-emails branch reuses user.email.invalid, so users blocked by admin action see the same message as malformed addresses and the new server-side distinction is dead weight; the new locale key has no consumer.

[ADVISORY] The spec suite for EmailValidator never exercises the whitelist/blacklist restriction branches that this diff moved into the new validator. The only tests (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) stub should_block? and run with both site restriction settings empty, so a regression in email_in_restriction_setting? (e.g. the hand-rolled regex escaping moved from user.rb) ships with zero coverage; sites relying on email_domains_blacklist would silently stop filtering.

[ADVISORY] The new client-side rejectedEmails behavior and the new users_controller error JSON shape (errors/values keys) have no test coverage anywhere in the diff. The gating condition `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` is verified by no spec or JS test; if user.errors.to_hash returns symbol keys in this Rails version, result.errors.email is undefined and the rejected-email UX silently never activates, a regression nobody would catch.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail table is shipped with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates blocked_emails, so operators cannot actually block any email. Site staff who need to block a user's email have no supported path to insert rows into blocked_emails; the feature is dead weight until a follow-up ships, and the match_count/last_match_at statistics can never be populated in production.

[BUG] The client discards the server's specific error message (user.email.blocked, 'is not allowed.') and re-renders every rejected email as the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') format-validation string. A user whose email was blocked by an admin sees 'user.email.invalid' (a format error) instead of the distinct 'user.email.blocked' message the server explicitly added to locales — the new locale string in server.en.yml is never surfaced on the client, making the new requirement 'comprehensive validation for blocked users' fail at the point of user communication.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs writes (increment match_count, save record) inside a validation callback, coupling a read-check to a side-effectful DB write on every user save with a changed email. Every failed signup or email change attempt with a listed email writes to blocked_emails even when the surrounding transaction rolls back (e.g. username also invalid), so match_count/last_match_at count validation attempts rather than actual blocks; and the round-trip save inside validation makes the validator non-idempotent and untestable without stubbing (as the spec is forced to do).

[ADVISORY] The server now returns errors/values hashes to all consumers of users#create, but the client-side rejectedEmails handling exists only in the create-account controller, so the new payload fields are used by exactly one caller while being shipped to all. Other consumers of the create response (omniauth-driven flows, other front-ends) receive new payload keys with no handling, and the growing rejectedEmails client list never clears on modal close — a user who sees 'email invalid', fixes nothing, closes, and reopens the modal still has stale rejections applied; the scope of the client work is narrower than the server contract change it accompanies.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no atomic SET match_count = match_count + 1 and no locking, so concurrent validations lose increments. Two users signing up with the same blocked email simultaneously each read match_count=5 and both write 6, undercounting the block statistics the table exists to collect; the counter permanently drifts from reality.

[BUG] should_block? executes record.save — a database write with full timestamps update — inside a model validation hook (EmailValidator.validate_each runs it on every User email validation), making validation a mutating side-effecting operation. Every failed-and-retried signup, every valid? call, and every spec that validates a User email increments match_count and bumps updated_at multiple times for one logical event, corrupting the statistics; any future caller that validates without persisting (e.g. admin previews) silently writes to the DB.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no downcasing anywhere in BlockedEmail, while User normalizes stored emails, so a blocked_emails row loaded with mixed-case case never matches. Operators who bulk-load the table with 'Bad@Spam.org' get zero blocks for users whose canonical email is bad@spam.org; the block list silently fails for any non-lowercase row.

[ADVISORY] Moving domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email enforcement into `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` gates all email rules on email_changed?, so a User record whose email was set before a domain was blacklisted (or before the address was blocked) continues to save cleanly with the now-forbidden email. Admins who add a domain to email_domains_blacklist expecting existing users to be forced off it on their next save see the setting apply only at signup time; the enforcement is weaker than the removed email_validator's same gate but now also silently skips BlockedEmail checks for any save path that doesn't change the email column (e.g. admin edit re-saving the same address).

[ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, controller action, rake task, or seed path inserts rows, so the feature ships inert. Operators cannot actually block any email without hand-writing SQL; the match_count/last_match_at instrumentation and the client-side rejectedEmails UX are dead code until a second, unbuilt change lands.

[ADVISORY] should_block? returns nil (from `record && ...` when record is nil) rather than false on the no-record path, conflating falsy sentinels for a public class method that reads like a predicate other code will treat with === false or serialize. Callers doing `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) == false` or logging the raw value get nil and mis-handle it; in Ruby this is latent, but any future consumer comparing explicitly gets silently wrong control flow.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})")` by naively interpolating the raw comma-separated setting, so a blacklist of 'mail.ru, spam.com' produces a regex matching '@(mail[.]ru, spam[.]com)' as a single literal alternation-free pattern with the comma embedded. This is carried over from the deleted User#email_in_restriction_setting?, but the diff re-homes the broken parser into a shared validator, entrenching it: any site setting with more than one domain never matches anything (whitelist) or never blocks anything (blacklist), and the next fix now has to change the new validator's public behavior.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes result.values.email (the server-normalized attribute) into rejectedEmails and compares it with .contains(email) against the raw accountEmail input, so the two sides of the membership check can differ in case/whitespace. A user whose typed input differs from the echoed value (e.g. trailing space preserved locally) is re-submitted to the server and re-rejected instead of being blocked client-side, defeating the feature's purpose for that user; the list also grows unboundedly across retries with no dedup beyond exact-match.

[BUG] The client replaces the server's specific email rejection reason with a generic 'user.email.invalid' message once an email enters rejectedEmails, discarding the original error text. A user whose email is rejected because it is already taken, or because of the whitelist/blacklist 'not allowed from that email provider' message, is shown 'is invalid' on every subsequent keystroke of that address — the original PR intent was surfacing blocked emails, but the implementation silently downgrades all server email errors (including pre-existing ones like uniqueness) to a generic invalid message.

[ADVISORY] rejectedEmails permanently blacklists an email for the life of the modal even when the server error was transient or user-fixable, with no path to clear it. If the server rejects an email for a time-dependent reason (e.g., a rate limit or a uniqueness conflict that is later resolved by the other account being renamed/deleted), the user can never resubmit the same address without closing and reopening the create-account dialog; the stated intent was blocking known-bad emails, not an unbounded client-side ban list.

[ADVISORY] The PR's stated objective (blocked-email validation) is bundled with a silent rewrite of the existing whitelist/blacklist email_validator into a new EmailValidator class, changing validation semantics without explicit acceptance. Operators relying on the old email_validator behavior now depend on an EachValidator that additionally runs BlockedEmail.should_block? (a DB read plus a write) inside every validation; the whitelist/blacklist logic moved from a model callback into lib/ with identical-looking but restructured code, so any future fix applied to the old location (the natural place someone familiar with the codebase would edit) is now dead code — a maintainability and drift hazard introduced alongside the feature rather than the feature itself.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive string match so a blocked email is trivially bypassed by varying letter case or other equivalent forms. An operator blocks 'spammer@example.com'; the spammer re-registers as 'Spammer@Example.com' or 'SPAMMER@example.com' and BlockedEmail.where(email: email) returns no row, so should_block? is false and signup succeeds — the entire blocklist control is defeated by a one-character case change (Rails' default uniqueness validation on the blocked_emails.email column is also case-sensitive, so the block entries themselves are stored in whatever case they were entered).

[ADVISORY] The whitelist/blacklist domain setting is interpolated unescaped into Regexp.new, so any regex metacharacter in the admin-set setting (commas separating domains, parentheses, '+', etc.) alters the pattern rather than matching literally. An admin entering 'gmail.com,yahoo.com' gets a pattern matching 'gmail\.com,yahoo\.com' only, silently failing to block yahoo.com; a setting containing '(' raises RegexpError and turns every account creation/email change into a 500 (caught as StatementInvalid-adjacent failure path, wrong error surfaced). This is carried over from the deleted user.rb code rather than newly introduced, but the diff chose to reproduce it in the new shared validator instead of fixing it.

[ADVISORY] The failed-signup response now echoes user.attributes.slice("name","username","email") plus the raw errors hash back to the anonymous client with no sanitization of the error messages themselves. Combined with the new EmailValidator, an unauthenticated visitor can probe whether a specific email address is on the server's blocklist or domain restrictions (distinct error strings 'not_allowed' vs 'blocked') and enumerate which usernames/emails are already taken, giving a free account-existence oracle on the public signup endpoint; the values payload also round-trips whatever the attacker submitted, slightly enlarging the reflection surface for any downstream XSS in the client error rendering.

[ADVISORY] The spec never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator (email_validator.rb:7-14), which contain the riskiest logic in the diff — the hand-built regexp from a raw setting string (gsub('.', '\.') + Regexp.new with interpolated, unescaped '|' semantics). Both tests run with email_domains_whitelist and email_domains_blacklist unset (default empty), so every line of email_in_restriction_setting? and both setting branches execute zero times; a regression in the migrated domain-restriction logic (e.g. dropping the elsif, breaking the escape, or inverting the whitelist test) ships with a green suite, and site operators relying on domain blacklists get unvalidated signups.

[BUG] The 'doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email' test passes even if the validator's entire BlockedEmail integration is deleted, because should_block? is stubbed and the negative case asserts only absence of errors. The stub means the test verifies the mock returns false, not that the validator consults it correctly: no assertion checks should_block? was actually invoked (an unused stub raises nothing in mocha), so removing the BlockedEmail call from email_validator.rb:16 or passing the wrong value to it leaves the negative test green while blocked-email enforcement silently stops for every non-blocked user — exactly the population the feature exists to police.

[ADVISORY] The short-circuit branch at email_validator.rb:16 — where a pre-existing restriction-setting error suppresses both the 'blocked' message and the should_block? match_count increment — has no test that triggers a domain-restriction failure together with a blocked email. Operators seeding blocked_emails and using a domain whitelist will see match_count/last_match_at stay frozen for emails that hit both rules, silently corrupting the abuse-tracking statistics the blocked_email_spec:31-38 tests document as the point of those columns; the spec only ever tests should_block? with a clean errors hash.

[ADVISORY] The 'returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist' test for should_block? relies on no prior spec creating the email, but the negative branch it asserts is only the nil-record path — the case where a record exists but save fails (validation race on the unique index, invalid action_type) is untested. should_block? returns record && record.action_type == actions[:block], so a failed save (e.g. concurrent insert hitting the unique index added in the migration) still returns the action verdict while losing the statistics write; a future maintainer changing should_block? to roll back on save failure has no test distinguishing intended behavior, and the mismatch between 'stats updated' shared example and the do_nothing:false path means the do_nothing context never asserts a block verdict is absent after a save failure.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (increment match_count, set last_match_at, save) inside the model validation path, so statistics are mutated as a side effect of validating a User. Every User.save with a changed email runs this write, even when the user record ultimately fails validation and is never created; validations also run multiple times per save in Rails, so match_count and last_match_at are inflated on rows that never correspond to real blocked signup attempts, and the 'has this email ever been blocked' signal the migration spec comments rely on is silently corrupted. A failed record.save() inside should_block? also raises ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid inside a validator, hitting the rescue in users_controller and masking the real validation error.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created with no writer path anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API, rake task, seed, or migration inserts rows. Operators deploying this cannot populate the blocklist; the EmailValidator's BlockedEmail.should_block? check matches nothing and the feature is inert until an out-of-band manual SQL load, which the spec comment ('if we manually load the table') implies is the intended workflow but is nowhere documented or tooled.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup uses an exact case-sensitive string match (where(email: email)) with no case-insensitive index or normalization, so 'Bad@Spamclub.com' bypasses a block on 'bad@spamclub.com' on case-sensitive collations (e.g. PostgreSQL). Users whose email differs only in local-part or domain case bypass the blocklist entirely; existing blocklist rows must be stored in exactly one casing and the enforcement silently misses variants.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? executes a blocking DB write (record.save) inside ActiveModel validation, so every validation run that touches a changed email increments match_count and updates last_match_at even when signup fails for unrelated reasons. match_count/last_match_at become meaningless as blocking statistics: any code path that validates or saves a user (repeated form submissions, username-taken retries, admin edits) inflates the counters, so an operator using these fields to judge which blocked addresses are actively abused gets fabricated numbers.

[BUG] The blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` uses a binary string comparison, and the controller-side user email is not normalized to the stored case. A blocked record for 'Spammer@Spam.org' fails to match 'spammer@spam.org', so a blocked spammer registers successfully by varying the case of their address — the entire blocking feature is bypassed with trivial effort.

[BUG] The `record.save` inside should_block? has its return value discarded, so a failed statistics write is silently swallowed and should_block? proceeds as though nothing happened. If the save fails (lock contention, stale record, serialization error), match_count and last_match_at silently stop advancing while signup validation continues to report success-shaped behavior, leaving operators with silently stale blocking data and no log line anywhere to detect it.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and model have no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. The feature ships inert: operators cannot actually block an email without manually inserting rows via SQL/console, so the new validation, locale string, migration, and frontend rejectedEmails handling are all dead code paths until an admin interface exists.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

The diff does not show any require/autoload-path change, so this can lead to “Unknown validator: EmailValidator” at runtime when validating a User.

The only writers visible are specs/fabricators. This makes the new blocking mechanism effectively unused unless the table is populated out-of-band (e.g., console), which is a completeness/usability concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb` the new validator hook is `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and `EmailValidator#validate_each` is where `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is called. That means the blocked-email enforcement only runs when Rails considers the email attribute “changed”, so a user whose email remains unchanged will not be re-checked against newly added `BlockedEmail` rows on later saves. This is diff-grounded and could be a hidden-coupling/semantic clarity issue, though the prior whitelist/blacklist logic was also conditional on `email_changed?`, so it’s not clearly a newly introduced break as much as an intentional/implicit policy that may surprise maintainers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `should_block?` mutates and `save`s the `BlockedEmail` record. However, the finding’s core claim (that this write is rolled back whenever the user save fails due to the email being blocked) is not supported by what’s shown: in Rails, validations run before the user’s persistence transaction (the `save` is short-circuited on validation failure), so there is no surrounding user-save transaction for the `BlockedEmail.save` to be rolled back with. The spec calling `should_block?` directly doesn’t imply a rollback issue either.

The added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only exercises the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch by stubbing it, and does not set either SiteSetting nor assert behavior for whitelist/blacklist. So the newly moved restriction logic is indeed untested by this new spec, leaving potential regressions in the regex/setting handling without coverage.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side logic (`rejectedEmails` array, early failure in `emailValidation`, and pushing `result.values.email` on server failure) and changes the controller failure JSON to include `errors` and `values`, but the only new specs cover `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`—there is no spec exercising `UsersController#create` failure JSON shape nor any JS/acceptance test covering the `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` gating and `rejectedEmails` behavior. The additional claim about `user.errors.to_hash` producing symbol keys causing `result.errors.email` to be undefined is not directly verifiable from the diff (JSON serialization typically stringifies keys), but the missing-test concern is concrete and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail table is shipped with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates blocked_emails, so operators cannot actually block any email. Site staff who need to block a user's email have no supported path to insert rows into blocked_emails; the feature is dead weight until a follow-up ships, and the match_count/last_match_at statistics can never be populated in production.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds the `blocked_emails` table/migration and uses it in `EmailValidator` via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but within this diff there’s no admin UI, controller endpoint, seed, or task to create/manage `BlockedEmail` rows—only a fabricator/spec. That makes the new blocking mechanism operationally incomplete unless operators manipulate the DB/console outside the app.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The client discards the server's specific error message (user.email.blocked, 'is not allowed.') and re-renders every rejected email as the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') format-validation string. A user whose email was blocked by an admin sees 'user.email.invalid' (a format error) instead of the distinct 'user.email.blocked' message the server explicitly added to locales — the new locale string in server.en.yml is never surfaced on the client, making the new requirement 'comprehensive validation for blocked users' fail at the point of user communication.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any previously rejected email is cached in `rejectedEmails` and then always fails validation with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (see the new `contains(email)` branch). The rejected email is added purely based on `result.errors.email` in the failure handler (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), without preserving/using the server-provided error key/message (e.g., `user.email.blocked` added in `server.en.yml` and produced by `EmailValidator`). Thus a blocked email (or any server-side email error) will be re-presented on the client as the generic `user.email.invalid` message rather than the specific server-side `user.email.blocked` reason.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs writes (increment match_count, save record) inside a validation callback, coupling a read-check to a side-effectful DB write on every user save with a changed email. Every failed signup or email change attempt with a listed email writes to blocked_emails even when the surrounding transaction rolls back (e.g. username also invalid), so match_count/last_match_at count validation attempts rather than actual blocks; and the round-trip save inside validation makes the validator non-idempotent and untestable without stubbing (as the spec is forced to do).

adjudication.rationale: Diff adds `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no other email errors exist (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `should_block?` performs side-effectful writes (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) on every validation hit for an existing blocked_email (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Since validations can run during a `User` save attempt that ultimately fails for other reasons (e.g. username/password), these writes can still occur even though the user record is never persisted, meaning the stats track validation attempts rather than successful blocks. This is a real design/architecture concern introduced by the change (non-idempotent validator, extra DB write during validation), but it’s not a clearly verifiable correctness defect because the behavior could be intentional for tracking attempts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The server now returns errors/values hashes to all consumers of users#create, but the client-side rejectedEmails handling exists only in the create-account controller, so the new payload fields are used by exactly one caller while being shipped to all. Other consumers of the create response (omniauth-driven flows, other front-ends) receive new payload keys with no handling, and the growing rejectedEmails client list never clears on modal close — a user who sees 'email invalid', fixes nothing, closes, and reopens the modal still has stale rejections applied; the scope of the client work is narrower than the server contract change it accompanies.

adjudication.rationale: The diff expands the failure JSON contract of `UsersController#create` to always include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb), but in this diff the only consumer that uses those new keys is the create-account modal controller, which checks `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` to populate `rejectedEmails` (create_account_controller.js). This is a real scope/contract concern (server change is broader than the client change), though the added keys are additive and not inherently breaking. Also, within the shown controller code `rejectedEmails` is only appended to and never reset/cleared anywhere (create_account_controller.js), which can lead to stale client-side rejection state if the controller instance persists across modal close/reopen, but that persistence cannot be verified from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no atomic SET match_count = match_count + 1 and no locking, so concurrent validations lose increments. Two users signing up with the same blocked email simultaneously each read match_count=5 and both write 6, undercounting the block statistics the table exists to collect; the counter permanently drifts from reality.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` loads a row (`where(email: email).first`), then does `record.match_count += 1` and `record.save`. This is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent calls can overwrite each other and lose increments (and potentially last_match_at updates) because there is no locking or atomic `UPDATE ... match_count = match_count + 1`/`update_counters` usage shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? executes record.save — a database write with full timestamps update — inside a model validation hook (EmailValidator.validate_each runs it on every User email validation), making validation a mutating side-effecting operation. Every failed-and-retried signup, every valid? call, and every spec that validates a User email increments match_count and bumps updated_at multiple times for one logical event, corrupting the statistics; any future caller that validates without persisting (e.g. admin previews) silently writes to the DB.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both point out that the email-block check method (should_block_email?/should_block?) performs database writes/updates (e.g., saving and incrementing statistics) during what should be a read-only check/validation, creating unintended side effects and potential concurrency/statistics corruption.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no downcasing anywhere in BlockedEmail, while User normalizes stored emails, so a blocked_emails row loaded with mixed-case case never matches. Operators who bulk-load the table with 'Bad@Spam.org' get zero blocks for users whose canonical email is bad@spam.org; the block list silently fails for any non-lowercase row.

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and neither BlockedEmail nor EmailValidator normalizes `email`/`value` (e.g., `downcase`) before querying. Given typical DB behavior (e.g., Postgres string equality is case-sensitive), a `blocked_emails.email` stored as mixed-case (e.g., `Bad@Spam.org`) will not match a differently-cased input (`bad@spam.org`), so blocks can be bypassed depending on casing. The diff shows no compensating case-insensitive query or normalization.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Moving domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email enforcement into `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` gates all email rules on email_changed?, so a User record whose email was set before a domain was blacklisted (or before the address was blocked) continues to save cleanly with the now-forbidden email. Admins who add a domain to email_domains_blacklist expecting existing users to be forced off it on their next save see the setting apply only at signup time; the enforcement is weaker than the removed email_validator's same gate but now also silently skips BlockedEmail checks for any save path that doesn't change the email column (e.g. admin edit re-saving the same address).

adjudication.rationale: In `User` the new validation `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (app/models/user.rb) means the new BlockedEmail enforcement inside `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) only runs when the email attribute changes, so an already-saved (now newly blocked) email won’t be rejected on saves that don’t modify `email`. However, the whitelist/blacklist behavior being gated by `email_changed?` is not newly introduced by this diff—the removed `email_validator` was also `if: :email_changed?`, so that part of the finding misattributes a regression.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, controller action, rake task, or seed path inserts rows, so the feature ships inert. Operators cannot actually block any email without hand-writing SQL; the match_count/last_match_at instrumentation and the client-side rejectedEmails UX are dead code until a second, unbuilt change lands.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `blocked_emails` (migration + `BlockedEmail` model) and enforces blocking via `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within this diff there is no production code path that creates/updates `BlockedEmail` rows (only specs/fabricator create records). So, based on the diff alone, operators would indeed have no built-in way to populate the table, making the new blocking feature operationally incomplete until another change adds a writer/UI/seed/task.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? returns nil (from `record && ...` when record is nil) rather than false on the no-record path, conflating falsy sentinels for a public class method that reads like a predicate other code will treat with === false or serialize. Callers doing `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) == false` or logging the raw value get nil and mis-handle it; in Ruby this is latent, but any future consumer comparing explicitly gets silently wrong control flow.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the last line is `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, which returns `nil` when no record is found. The diff’s own spec expects an actual `false` in that case (`subject.should be_false` in `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`), so this is a real behavioral mismatch/defect introduced by the new method implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})")` by naively interpolating the raw comma-separated setting, so a blacklist of 'mail.ru, spam.com' produces a regex matching '@(mail[.]ru, spam[.]com)' as a single literal alternation-free pattern with the comma embedded. This is carried over from the deleted User#email_in_restriction_setting?, but the diff re-homes the broken parser into a shared validator, entrenching it: any site setting with more than one domain never matches anything (whitelist) or never blocks anything (blacklist), and the next fix now has to change the new validator's public behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The new shared validator in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` implements `email_in_restriction_setting?` as `domains = setting.gsub('.', '\.')` and `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. If `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `blacklist` contains a comma-separated list (e.g., `"mail.ru, spam.com"`), this produces a regex like `@(mail\.ru, spam\.com)` which matches the literal comma/space sequence rather than alternation, so multi-domain lists won’t work as intended. This logic is present in the diff and affects correctness of whitelist/blacklist behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client pushes result.values.email (the server-normalized attribute) into rejectedEmails and compares it with .contains(email) against the raw accountEmail input, so the two sides of the membership check can differ in case/whitespace. A user whose typed input differs from the echoed value (e.g. trailing space preserved locally) is re-submitted to the server and re-rejected instead of being blocked client-side, defeating the feature's purpose for that user; the list also grows unboundedly across retries with no dedup beyond exact-match.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new client-side short-circuit checks `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` where `email` is `accountEmail` from the input, but on failure it pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). Since the diff shows no normalization/trim/case-folding on either side, the cached rejected value can differ from the user’s current raw input (e.g., whitespace/case differences), causing the membership check to miss and allowing repeated submissions/rejections. Also, `pushObject` can add duplicates unless the string matches exactly, so the list can grow across retries.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The client replaces the server's specific email rejection reason with a generic 'user.email.invalid' message once an email enters rejectedEmails, discarding the original error text. A user whose email is rejected because it is already taken, or because of the whitelist/blacklist 'not allowed from that email provider' message, is shown 'is invalid' on every subsequent keystroke of that address — the original PR intent was surfacing blocked emails, but the implementation silently downgrades all server email errors (including pre-existing ones like uniqueness) to a generic invalid message.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, once an email is added to `rejectedEmails`, `emailMatch` immediately returns a failed `InputValidation` with the hardcoded reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` whenever `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` (new block around `if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)) { ... reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid') }`). The email gets added on any server-side email error (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`), not just the newly introduced blocked-email case. This means subsequent validations for that same email will show the generic "invalid" message rather than the specific server error (e.g., uniqueness taken, `user.email.not_allowed`, or the new `user.email.blocked`). The diff directly supports the finding that specific rejection reasons are downgraded after the first failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] rejectedEmails permanently blacklists an email for the life of the modal even when the server error was transient or user-fixable, with no path to clear it. If the server rejects an email for a time-dependent reason (e.g., a rate limit or a uniqueness conflict that is later resolved by the other account being renamed/deleted), the user can never resubmit the same address without closing and reopening the create-account dialog; the stated intent was blocking known-bad emails, not an unbounded client-side ban list.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, `rejectedEmails` is initialized once (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`) and any server-side create failure that includes `result.errors.email` causes the submitted email to be pushed into this array (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). Subsequent validations short-circuit and always fail if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`, returning `user.email.invalid`, with no code path in the diff to remove/clear entries. Therefore, within the lifetime of the modal/controller instance, the same email cannot be resubmitted even if the original server-side email error was transient or later resolved.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The PR's stated objective (blocked-email validation) is bundled with a silent rewrite of the existing whitelist/blacklist email_validator into a new EmailValidator class, changing validation semantics without explicit acceptance. Operators relying on the old email_validator behavior now depend on an EachValidator that additionally runs BlockedEmail.should_block? (a DB read plus a write) inside every validation; the whitelist/blacklist logic moved from a model callback into lib/ with identical-looking but restructured code, so any future fix applied to the old location (the natural place someone familiar with the codebase would edit) is now dead code — a maintainability and drift hazard introduced alongside the feature rather than the feature itself.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly replaces the model-level `validate :email_validator` + `email_validator/email_in_restriction_setting?` methods in `app/models/user.rb` with a new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` `ActiveModel::EachValidator` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). That is a nontrivial refactor bundled with the blocked-email feature. The new validator also calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (which does a query plus mutating `save` via `match_count`/`last_match_at`) during validation, introducing side effects and potential perf/behavior considerations beyond the stated feature. This is a concrete scope/maintainability concern grounded in the diff, not a directly provable correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive string match so a blocked email is trivially bypassed by varying letter case or other equivalent forms. An operator blocks 'spammer@example.com'; the spammer re-registers as 'Spammer@Example.com' or 'SPAMMER@example.com' and BlockedEmail.where(email: email) returns no row, so should_block? is false and signup succeeds — the entire blocklist control is defeated by a one-character case change (Rails' default uniqueness validation on the blocked_emails.email column is also case-sensitive, so the block entries themselves are stored in whatever case they were entered).
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same underlying issue: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a case-sensitive exact email lookup, allowing blocked users to bypass by changing letter case (e.g., User@Example.com vs user@example.com), defeating the blocklist and enabling unauthorized signups.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The whitelist/blacklist domain setting is interpolated unescaped into Regexp.new, so any regex metacharacter in the admin-set setting (commas separating domains, parentheses, '+', etc.) alters the pattern rather than matching literally. An admin entering 'gmail.com,yahoo.com' gets a pattern matching 'gmail\.com,yahoo\.com' only, silently failing to block yahoo.com; a setting containing '(' raises RegexpError and turns every account creation/email change into a 500 (caught as StatementInvalid-adjacent failure path, wrong error surfaced). This is carried over from the deleted user.rb code rather than newly introduced, but the diff chose to reproduce it in the new shared validator instead of fixing it.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `email_in_restriction_setting?` builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` from the admin-provided `SiteSetting` after only `gsub('.', '\.')`. Any other regex metacharacters or separators in the setting (e.g., `,`, `(`, `+`, `|`) are not escaped, so the regex can behave incorrectly (e.g., comma-separated domains won’t match as intended) or even raise `RegexpError` on invalid patterns, causing account creation/email validation to error. This logic is directly present in the diff and was reintroduced into the shared validator unchanged.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The failed-signup response now echoes user.attributes.slice("name","username","email") plus the raw errors hash back to the anonymous client with no sanitization of the error messages themselves. Combined with the new EmailValidator, an unauthenticated visitor can probe whether a specific email address is on the server's blocklist or domain restrictions (distinct error strings 'not_allowed' vs 'blocked') and enumerate which usernames/emails are already taken, giving a free account-existence oracle on the public signup endpoint; the values payload also round-trips whatever the attacker submitted, slightly enlarging the reflection surface for any downstream XSS in the client error rendering.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name","username","email")` for an anonymous signup attempt. The new `EmailValidator` can add distinct error strings (`I18n.t(:'user.email.not_allowed')` vs `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')`, with `user.email.blocked` added to locales), meaning the public endpoint can reveal whether an email hit domain restrictions vs the new blocklist (`BlockedEmail.should_block?`). Additionally, exposing the raw `errors` hash will include uniqueness validation messages for `email`/`username` (`validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`), enabling straightforward account existence probing. The `values` echo also reflects attacker-supplied fields back to the client, increasing exposure if any client-side rendering is unsafe (the reflection itself is shown in the diff).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The spec never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator (email_validator.rb:7-14), which contain the riskiest logic in the diff — the hand-built regexp from a raw setting string (gsub('.', '\.') + Regexp.new with interpolated, unescaped '|' semantics). Both tests run with email_domains_whitelist and email_domains_blacklist unset (default empty), so every line of email_in_restriction_setting? and both setting branches execute zero times; a regression in the migrated domain-restriction logic (e.g. dropping the elsif, breaking the escape, or inverting the whitelist test) ships with a green suite, and site operators relying on domain blacklists get unvalidated signups.

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator#validate_each` has three main branches: whitelist (`SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`), blacklist (`SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`), and the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` check. The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only covers the blocked-email behavior by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and does not set either `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`, so lines 7–14 and `email_in_restriction_setting?` (regex construction from the raw setting string) are never executed. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap for logic that was migrated from `User#email_validator` into the validator and could regress without failing the suite.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email' test passes even if the validator's entire BlockedEmail integration is deleted, because should_block? is stubbed and the negative case asserts only absence of errors. The stub means the test verifies the mock returns false, not that the validator consults it correctly: no assertion checks should_block? was actually invoked (an unused stub raises nothing in mocha), so removing the BlockedEmail call from email_validator.rb:16 or passing the wrong value to it leaves the negative test green while blocked-email enforcement silently stops for every non-blocked user — exactly the population the feature exists to police.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, the negative-case test stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? to return false but only asserts record.errors[:email] is blank. With mocha `stubs`, an unused stub does not fail, so the test would still pass if the validator stopped calling BlockedEmail.should_block? (or passed a wrong value) because no error would be added anyway. This is a specific, diff-grounded weakness in the new test coverage rather than a production defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The short-circuit branch at email_validator.rb:16 — where a pre-existing restriction-setting error suppresses both the 'blocked' message and the should_block? match_count increment — has no test that triggers a domain-restriction failure together with a blocked email. Operators seeding blocked_emails and using a domain whitelist will see match_count/last_match_at stay frozen for emails that hit both rules, silently corrupting the abuse-tracking statistics the blocked_email_spec:31-38 tests document as the point of those columns; the spec only ever tests should_block? with a clean errors hash.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is only called when `record.errors[attribute].blank?` (line with `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), so a whitelist/blacklist failure will prevent both the blocked-message addition and the `should_block?` side effects (match_count/last_match_at updates in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`). The added specs (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` and `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`) do not cover the combined case where a domain restriction error exists *and* the email is in `blocked_emails`, so the finding about a missing test for this interaction is grounded. Whether stats should increment even when another validation already fails is a product/logic decision, so this is best classified as an important edge-case/test gap rather than a clearly provable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The 'returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist' test for should_block? relies on no prior spec creating the email, but the negative branch it asserts is only the nil-record path — the case where a record exists but save fails (validation race on the unique index, invalid action_type) is untested. should_block? returns record && record.action_type == actions[:block], so a failed save (e.g. concurrent insert hitting the unique index added in the migration) still returns the action verdict while losing the statistics write; a future maintainer changing should_block? to roll back on save failure has no test distinguishing intended behavior, and the mismatch between 'stats updated' shared example and the do_nothing:false path means the do_nothing context never asserts a block verdict is absent after a save failure.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the only write is `record.save` on an existing row fetched by `where(email: email).first`; the finding’s example of a “concurrent insert hitting the unique index added in the migration” doesn’t apply to this update path (it’s not creating a `blocked_emails` row). Also, `action_type` has no validation in the diff, so “invalid action_type” causing `save` failure isn’t shown. The specs do only cover the nil-record branch and the normal save/update branches, but the finding’s save-failure scenarios and claimed race/validation causes are not grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (increment match_count, set last_match_at, save) inside the model validation path, so statistics are mutated as a side effect of validating a User. Every User.save with a changed email runs this write, even when the user record ultimately fails validation and is never created; validations also run multiple times per save in Rails, so match_count and last_match_at are inflated on rows that never correspond to real blocked signup attempts, and the 'has this email ever been blocked' signal the migration spec comments rely on is silently corrupted. A failed record.save() inside should_block? also raises ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid inside a validator, hitting the rescue in users_controller and masking the real validation error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator` which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during validation (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`). `should_block?` does a read-modify-write side effect (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s) whenever a matching blocked_email row exists (`app/models/blocked_email.rb`). Because this is executed in the User validation path (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`), it will mutate blocked_email statistics even when the user ultimately fails other validations or when validations are run multiple times, inflating/corrupting the tracking fields the model/specs imply are meaningful.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created with no writer path anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API, rake task, seed, or migration inserts rows. Operators deploying this cannot populate the blocklist; the EmailValidator's BlockedEmail.should_block? check matches nothing and the feature is inert until an out-of-band manual SQL load, which the spec comment ('if we manually load the table') implies is the intended workflow but is nowhere documented or tooled.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `blocked_emails` (migration/model) and enforces blocking via `EmailValidator` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but there is no code in this diff providing any mechanism to create/manage `BlockedEmail` rows (no controller/admin UI/API/task/seed). As a result, deployments using only this change would have an inert blocklist unless operators manually insert rows (which is hinted at by the spec comment about manually loading the table). This is a completeness/operability concern grounded in the diff, not a correctness bug in the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup uses an exact case-sensitive string match (where(email: email)) with no case-insensitive index or normalization, so 'Bad@Spamclub.com' bypasses a block on 'bad@spamclub.com' on case-sensitive collations (e.g. PostgreSQL). Users whose email differs only in local-part or domain case bypass the blocklist entirely; existing blocklist rows must be stored in exactly one casing and the enforcement silently misses variants.

adjudication.rationale: The new block check is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, and the validator passes the raw `value` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) with no downcasing/normalization and no case-insensitive lookup/index shown. On case-sensitive comparisons (e.g., PostgreSQL), this means a stored block row for `bad@spamclub.com` will not match `Bad@Spamclub.com`, so the block can be bypassed purely by casing differences.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? executes a blocking DB write (record.save) inside ActiveModel validation, so every validation run that touches a changed email increments match_count and updates last_match_at even when signup fails for unrelated reasons. match_count/last_match_at become meaningless as blocking statistics: any code path that validates or saves a user (repeated form submissions, username-taken retries, admin edits) inflates the counters, so an operator using these fields to judge which blocked addresses are actively abused gets fabricated numbers.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when there are no prior email errors. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) every time a blocked email is *validated*, regardless of whether the overall user creation/update succeeds or fails later for other reasons. This is a real diff-grounded concern (side effects + noisy/inflated statistics), but it doesn't clearly break core functionality (blocking still works), so it’s better classified as a non-bug design/behavior issue rather than a definite correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` uses a binary string comparison, and the controller-side user email is not normalized to the stored case. A blocked record for 'Spammer@Spam.org' fails to match 'spammer@spam.org', so a blocked spammer registers successfully by varying the case of their address — the entire blocking feature is bypassed with trivial effort.

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and the validator passes the raw submitted value (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) without any normalization (no `downcase`, no `LOWER(email)` query, no case-insensitive index). That means the blocking check depends on the database’s string comparison semantics and can fail to match the same email with different casing, potentially bypassing the new blocked-email feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The `record.save` inside should_block? has its return value discarded, so a failed statistics write is silently swallowed and should_block? proceeds as though nothing happened. If the save fails (lock contention, stale record, serialization error), match_count and last_match_at silently stop advancing while signup validation continues to report success-shaped behavior, leaving operators with silently stale blocking data and no log line anywhere to detect it.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` and calls `record.save` without checking the boolean return value (and without logging). That’s a valid robustness/observability concern: if `save` were ever to return `false`, the stats update would be silently skipped while the method still returns based on `record.action_type`. However, based on the diff, a `false` return is unlikely here (the record already exists and validations are simple), and typical DB failures (lock/serialization) would raise exceptions rather than be silently swallowed. So it’s not a clearly verifiable functional defect, but it is a concrete review issue grounded in the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and model have no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. The feature ships inert: operators cannot actually block an email without manually inserting rows via SQL/console, so the new validation, locale string, migration, and frontend rejectedEmails handling are all dead code paths until an admin interface exists.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and wires it into validation via `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), plus frontend handling for rejected emails. However, within this diff there is no admin UI, controller endpoint, rake task, seed, or other code path that creates/updates `blocked_emails` records outside of tests/fabricators. That means the feature is effectively operator-unfriendly/incomplete unless rows are manually inserted via console/SQL. This is a real scope/completeness concern grounded in the diff, but not a correctness bug in the code shown.
